seoTitle: Namecheap Private Email: Pricing, Setup and the Free Trial
metaDescription: Use Namecheap Private Email the right way. Compare the Starter, Pro and Ultimate plans, claim the 30-day free trial, create your mailbox and connect it to Outlook or Gmail.
intro:
Namecheap Private Email is a cheap way to get an inbox on your own domain, but the pricing page is doing a lot at once: three tiers, a promo code sitting in a box, a first-term price that looks nothing like the renewal price, and a trial that makes the first month free. Get those pieces straight and a branded address costs a couple of dollars a month. Miss them and you pay several times more than needed at renewal.

This guide walks the real path: finding Private Email inside your Namecheap account, reading the plan table for what differs, claiming the free trial, then creating the mailbox and wiring it into the mail app you already use. Along the way it flags the two numbers most people skip, the renewal rate and the mailbox count, since those decide whether the plan you pick still fits in a year.

steps.heading: Find Private Email inside your Namecheap account
steps.body:
Private Email is a product you manage from your account dashboard, not something buried in a domain's settings. Sign in, and the left-hand rail lists Domain List, Hosting List, Private Email, SSL Certificates, Apps, My Offers and Profile. Private Email sits third, and that one link is the hub for buying, assigning and managing every mailbox on your account. Your domains are listed to the right with their status, expiry date and a Manage button on each row, which matters because a Private Email subscription has to be attached to a domain you control before mail will flow.

If the domain is registered with Namecheap, as the one shown here is, the connection is close to automatic. If it's registered elsewhere, plan on editing MX records at your current DNS host after you subscribe.

image.caption: The Namecheap account dashboard. Private Email has its own entry in the left rail, separate from the domain list beside it.

steps.heading: Read the three plans for what differs
steps.body:
Private Email comes in Starter, Pro and Ultimate, and the difference between them is mailboxes and storage, not core features. Starter is one mailbox with 5GB, Pro is three mailboxes with 30GB, and Ultimate is five mailboxes with 75GB plus document tools and premium delivery. Every tier gets mobile sync, so you aren't paying more just to read mail on your phone.

Pick by how many people need their own login. One person running a business usually needs only Starter, because aliases (covered further down) cover you@, hello@ and support@ without buying extra mailboxes. Buying Pro when a single mailbox with three aliases would do the same job is the most common overspend on this page.

image.caption: The Private Email plan table with the MAILDEAL promo code already filled in on each tier, and the first-year and renewal prices spelled out underneath.

steps.heading: Apply the promo code and check the renewal price
steps.body:
Namecheap pre-fills a promo code on the pricing page (MAILDEAL in the run shown here), and each plan shows what it saves: roughly 33 percent off Ultimate, 28 percent off Pro and 20 percent off Starter. Copy it with the button beside the box and confirm it's in the cart field at checkout, since the discount doesn't follow you automatically from every entry point.

Then read the small line under the button, which is the number that matters most. In this run, Starter billed at $11.88 for the first year and renewed at $14.88, Pro at $29.98 renewing at $41.88, and Ultimate at $47.88 renewing at $71.88. Promo codes and percentages rotate, so treat the exact figures as a snapshot; the structure of a discounted first term followed by a higher renewal stays the same. The renewal prices are the ones to budget against, not the first-year ones.

steps.heading: Start the free trial before you pay anything
steps.body:
The Trial tab on the pricing page is how you get Private Email for free. When a trial is running, checkout shows $0.00 for the first month instead of the plan's usual price. You still complete checkout and a card is still recorded, so the habit worth building is noting the date the trial converts and the renewal amount printed under the button.

The trial has real limits: it caps outgoing mail at 20 messages per hour per mailbox, blocks you from buying additional mailboxes until you upgrade, and can only be used once per domain. Use the month for the thing a feature list can't tell you: send and receive real mail, check that messages to Gmail and Outlook recipients land in the inbox instead of spam, and try the webmail on your phone. If the trial has ended by the time you read this, the paid Starter plan is cheap enough that the decision barely changes.

steps.heading: Create the mailbox and get mail flowing
steps.body:
After checkout, open Private Email from the dashboard rail and create the mailbox itself. You choose the local part of the address, the domain it belongs to, and a password, and that combination is your webmail login as well as the credentials any mail app will use. A subscription with unused mailboxes shows them as empty slots you can fill later, so on Pro or Ultimate you can add a teammate's address without buying anything more.

Mail won't arrive until the domain's MX records point at Namecheap's mail servers. For a domain registered with Namecheap this is applied for you when you link the subscription; for a domain hosted elsewhere, copy the MX values from the Private Email setup screen into your existing DNS provider. Give DNS changes a few minutes to settle, then send yourself a test message from an outside address before putting the new address on anything public.

steps.heading: Connect it to Outlook or Gmail
steps.body:
Webmail works for a quick check, but most people want the branded address inside the client they already use. Both Outlook and Gmail take the same three things: your full email address as the username, your mailbox password, and Namecheap's incoming and outgoing server names with their SSL ports, all listed on the Private Email setup page.

In Gmail, add it under Settings, Accounts and Import: POP or IMAP for receiving, and "Send mail as" with the SMTP details so replies leave from the branded address instead of your Gmail one. Choose IMAP over POP unless you have a specific reason not to; IMAP keeps the same folder state across your laptop, phone and webmail instead of pulling messages onto one device. Mobile sync on every tier is what makes the phone side work cleanly here.

steps.heading: Add aliases, spam filtering and calendar sync
steps.body:
Once mail flows, the features that make one cheap mailbox feel like a full email system are worth ten minutes. Aliases let addresses like support@ and billing@ deliver into the inbox you already pay for, which is how a Starter plan can cover a whole small business.

The anti-spam layer sits in its own tab on the pricing page and runs by default, but check the quarantine in the first week so you know what it's holding back before a customer's mail goes missing. Calendar and contacts sync over the same account, so adding the mailbox to your phone brings the calendar with it. Keep an eye on storage too; 5GB fills faster than expected once attachments pile up, and clearing large mail beats upgrading a tier you didn't need.

costNote: Every tier renews well above its first-term price, so budget against the renewal figure printed under the plan, not the discounted number on the promo banner. The trial is genuinely free for the first month, not just cheap, but it still runs through checkout and records a card on file.

tables.note: First-year and renewal prices depend on the promo code running when you buy; check the line under each plan's button at checkout instead of treating these as fixed.

faq.question: Can I get Namecheap Private Email for free?
faq.answer: Yes, when a trial is running. The Trial tab on the Private Email pricing page drops checkout to $0.00 for the first month. You still complete checkout, and the plan converts to the printed renewal rate once the trial ends.

faq.question: How long does the Namecheap Private Email trial last?
faq.answer: One month. During it, outgoing mail is capped at 20 messages per hour per mailbox and you can't buy additional mailboxes until you upgrade to a paid plan. It can only be used once per domain.

faq.question: How much does Namecheap Private Email cost?
faq.answer: Renewal rates run around $14.88 a year for Starter, $41.88 for Pro and $71.88 for Ultimate, with promo codes discounting the first term below that. Codes and rates rotate, so check the line under each plan's button for the current figures.

faq.question: What's the difference between Starter, Pro and Ultimate?
faq.answer: Mailboxes and storage, mainly: 1 mailbox and 5GB, 3 mailboxes and 30GB, or 5 mailboxes and 75GB. Ultimate adds document tools and premium email delivery. Mobile sync is included on all three.

faq.question: Can I use Namecheap Private Email with Gmail or Outlook?
faq.answer: Yes. Add the account in your client using your full address as the username, your mailbox password, and the IMAP and SMTP server details from the Private Email setup page. In Gmail, set up "Send mail as" too so replies go out from the branded address.

faq.question: Do I need my domain registered at Namecheap to use Private Email?
faq.answer: No. A domain registered with Namecheap links almost automatically, but a domain hosted anywhere else works too, once you copy the MX records from the Private Email setup screen into your existing DNS provider.

Renewal prices ($14.88 / $41.88 / $71.88 for Starter/Pro/Ultimate) matched Namecheap's published additional-mailbox pricing page.
